zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid: [NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, version 202510](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida, licensed [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Consulted after independent scan reading; the transcription and English review notes are reviewer-authored, and the supplied scan remains the authority.

lines.note: Teihatsu means shaving the head; kami soru gives the Japanese paraphrase, and rapar a cabeça supplies the Portuguese equivalent. The checked final t is retained without expanding it to a modern syllable.
Teihei is glossed as a strong, robust soldier. The headword's period is upright; italic type begins with Soldado, correcting the draft's misplaced style boundary.

Teigetsu denotes the last day of the month. The synonym visibly reads Tçumogori here; although tsugomori is the expected Japanese identification, the transposed-looking printed syllables are retained rather than silently repaired.
Do mes completes the preceding definition as the last day of the month. This short continuation remains a separate physical row.

runs.text: Couſas, que o Reyfaz, ou ordena.

lines.note: Teigyoo covers the king's actions or ordinances. The circumflex and the closely set Reyfaz are retained as printed, rather than changing the vowel category or regularizing the spacing.
Teiji is explained by hissage motsu, holding something hanging from the hand. The Portuguese de- begins dependurada on the following row.
Completes dependurada na mão: suspended in the hand. The final upright S. labels the expression as written usage and is separated from the italic gloss.
Teijo is explained as tadashii onna, a virtuous woman, and glossed as a good, chaste woman. The historical molher spelling and the initial v of vonna are preserved.
Teijuu denotes reverence and hospitable reception. The long-u mark has two converging strokes, matching the caron in the repeated example below rather than the draft's grave accent.
Teijuu wo itasu means showing reverence or respectful hospitality. The Portuguese verb agaſalhar is divided after agaſa-, with the visible terminal hyphen retained.
Completes agaſalhar com reſpeito, receiving or treating someone with respect. It closes the example begun on the preceding row.
Teizen is explained by niwa no mae, the space before the courtyard or garden. Niua is a Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese definition; its local italic presentation is retained.
Teizen no hana names the flowers before or in the courtyard. The gloss uses both rosas and the printed historical fulas; Niua is the Japanese term embedded in that Portuguese explanation.
Teijitsu is defined as certain, settled truth. The final S. is an upright written-register label, while the Portuguese definition remains italic.
Teinei denotes warmth of reception and affection in this entry. The divided Tei- starts the example teinei wo tsukusu on the next row.
Completes teinei wo tsukusu, extending abundant courtesy or hospitality. The Portuguese makes the hospitable-action sense explicit rather than restricting the word to modern politeness.
Teineini is the adverb: in a friendly or affectionate manner. The italic grammatical label Adu. and divided amo- belong to the Portuguese explanation.
Completes amorosamente and adds abundant hospitality or affectionate welcome. The row continues the adverbial gloss and introduces no new headword.
Teineisa is the noun for affection and hospitable treatment. The scan shows the descending g of agaſalhado, correcting the OCR's açaſalhado.

Teiketsu denotes the imperial palace, glossed as the paços of the Dairi. Dayri is a Japanese institutional title embedded in the Portuguese definition; the worn headword remains legible from its surviving types.

Teikyuu is weeping, explained by naki/naku and Portuguese chorar. The h and o of chorar correct OCR chirar; S. is upright. Fot- begins the compound hotsuro teikyuu, whose checked-coda t precedes ro on the next physical row.

Completes Fot-/ro, teiqiǔ, identifiable as hotsuro teikyuu, penitential weeping. The bare t in Fotro is a regular historical checked coda, not a missing syllable to be repaired. Lexical comparison: Shogakukan, Seisenban Nihon Kokugo Daijiten, [発露啼泣](https://kotobank.jp/word/発露啼泣-2082649), accessed after the independent scan reading; the printed comma and division remain unchanged.
Teiro means displaying something held suspended, as hissage arawasu explains. The Portuguese cou-/ſa is divided across physical rows, and the visible terminal hyphen is retained.
Completes couſa dependurada na mão, something hanging in the hand. The upright S. marks written usage and is not part of the italic Portuguese sentence.
Teitaku, alternatively teitoo, is an adverb meaning forcefully. The Latin l gives an alternative form; the caron over the second form's o is visibly distinct from a circumflex.
Impeto completes com força, & impeto: with force and impetus. The single-word continuation remains its own physical line.

Teitai is impediment or delay, explained by Japanese verbs for stopping and becoming held up. Enlarged reinspection supports the abraded a in Todomari: part of its left bowl remains and no i-dot is present. This qualified correction replaces Todomiri; printed todocouoru and the divided Portuguese impedido are preserved.
Completes impedido, followed by detido, being impeded or detained. S. is the upright label for written usage.

Teitaraku denotes manner, condition, or appearance here. The damaged initial is T, supported by its surviving top and repeated teitaracu below, rather than the OCR's F; Co- starts kono in the example.
Completes kono sekai no teitaraku, the condition or manner of this world. Portuguese modo, ou maneira begins the corresponding paraphrase.
Completes the explanation as how the world stands or is constituted. The printed grave accent in eſtà is preserved.
Teito is equated with miyako, the imperial capital. The Portuguese explains it as the court or chief city, with the location of the sovereign supplied on the next row.
Completes the capital-city definition as the place where the king resides. It belongs to Teito and is not a separate entry.
Teitoo here means strongly and impetuously. The caron marks this adverb and should not be assimilated to the circumflex of the different entry for order below.
Teitoo kassen suru illustrates fighting with force. The Japanese suru corresponds to Portuguese pellejar, and the manner of fighting continues on the following row.
Rijamente completes the example's description of forceful, vigorous fighting. This short row closes the adverbial Teitǒ entry.
Teitoo in this separate entry means order or sequence, also in shidai teitoo. Both printed o marks point upward and are retained as circumflexes, distinct from the preceding carons.
Teitoku means imperial virtue, explicitly paraphrased as teioo no toku. The visible t and c correct the garbled OCR Teiocu; the Portuguese list continues below.

runs.text: partes do Rey, que gouerna bem, &c.

lines.note: Completes the description of the virtues and good qualities of a king who governs well. Partes is used for personal qualities in this Portuguese explanation.
Teioo is a king or emperor. The caron remains visible despite its close alignment with the o, and emperador retains the historical spelling.
Teisei is explained as the emperor's capital. The scan supports Corte, the royal court, rather than OCR Certe; its alternate city definition continues below.

runs.text: cidade principal onde reſide o Rey.

lines.note: Completes the explanation as the chief city where the king resides. The repeated royal-capital wording agrees with teioo no miyako above.

This Teisei entry concerns a crying voice, naku koe, rather than the capital. Choroſa is supported by the surviving letters and the bilingual sense, though the o after r is abraded; the written-register S. is upright.

Teishin here denotes a dependable vassal or retainer, tashikana shinka. The Portuguese specifies a loyal servant of the king; the damaged middle of xinca is retained from the surviving word and its clear repetition below.
Extends the preceding loyal-retainer definition to another lord as well as the king. It is a short continuation of the same entry.
This separate Teishin entry combines mikado and shinka, sovereign and vassal. The Portuguese pair rey and vaſallo confirms the two-party meaning.

Teishin is the faithful or upright heart, tadashii kokoro, glossed as fidelity. The damaged headword ending, daxij, cocoro, and Fidelidade are restored from surviving strokes and bilingual agreement; Itẽ opens the chastity sense at the top of column 2.
Continues the Teixin entry from the foot of column 1 with chastity and purity. Teishin wo mamoru begins here, literally preserving one's fidelity or chastity, with mamoru divided across rows.
Moru completes mamoru; the Portuguese translates the full expression as being chaste. This is a continuation of the preceding entry, not a headword moru.
Teishinna describes a faithful and loyal person. The ending na forms the adjectival expression derived from the immediately preceding sense of teishin.
Teishoo is explained by niwa no ue, the courtyard or the space in it. Niua is repeated as a Japanese term inside the Portuguese definition, which continues with pateo below.
Pateo completes the courtyard definition. Teishoo ni kashikomaru describes adopting a respectful crouching posture in the courtyard; the Portuguese expression continues into cocaras.
Completes estar em cocaras no pateo, being crouched in the courtyard. The printed cocaras is retained without supplying a modern accent or an expected extra letter.
This separate Teishoo is explained by utena no ue, on a raised seat or platform. The Portuguese specifies being above or on a throne and then broadens the definition below.
Extends the definition to some high and splendid place. Dalgũ abbreviates the nasal ending and is preserved exactly rather than expanded.
Teishu is the master of the house, explicitly equated with ie no nushi. The gloss concerns household authority; it does not require importing the modern narrower sense of husband.
Tezei denotes one's own men or soldiers. Proprios distinguishes a person's own following from soldiers in general.

runs.text: Arte, & meneo das mãos como em

lines.note: Tejina here is skill and movement of the hands. The examples that follow are dancing and using a fan, so the definition should not be narrowed automatically to modern stage magic.
Completes the examples of manual skill: dancing or handling a fan. Abano is the printed Portuguese word for the fan, and the clause remains part of Tejina.

Tejita denotes something lesser or inferior. The example begins with a damaged or anomalously shortened T- before vye below; teue is contextually expected, but no e is supplied where this impression does not establish it.

Continues the contrast of upper and lower things, teue and tejita. The physical T-/vye spelling is retained with the preceding caveat, while the Portuguese translates the contrast as high and low or inferior.
Feriores completes inferiores from the preceding in-. It closes the definition of the contrasted lower things.

runs.text: Iornal, ou paga, que ſe dà a algum

lines.note: Temachin denotes a daily wage or payment for labour. Portuguese Iornal is the historical wage term, and the following rows specify the worker who receives it.

runs.text: official, ou a algum homem alugado pera tra-

lines.note: Specifies payment to a craftsman or a man hired to work. The visible lowercase tra- corrects OCR Ira- and begins trabalhar on the next row.
Balhar completes trabalhar, the work performed by the hired man. This short fragment belongs to the wage definition.
Temaryoo is given in competing eô and iô spellings, both referring to the preceding payment for labour. The two circumflexes are visible and remain distinct from nearby carons.

runs.text: Pela que ſe joga com a mão. ¶

lines.note: Temari is a ball played with the hand. The repeated name begins the example at the right edge, with a visible terminal hyphen after Te-.

runs.text: Iugar à pela com a mão.

lines.note: Completes temari wo tsuku, bouncing or playing with a handball. The Portuguese Iugar retains its printed historical initial and spelling.
Temarika is identified only as a white rose or flower. The definition does not by itself justify a more precise botanical identification, and the printed fula is retained.
Temasari and temasarina are equated with temashi. Vide begins the Portuguese cross-reference directing the reader to the fuller entry below.
Infrà completes Vide infrà, see below. It belongs to the preceding cross-reference and remains a separate physical row with its printed grave accent.
Tematai describes a simple and upright person. The two indented forms below belong to this entry rather than being definitions accidentally omitted by the OCR.
Tematasa is the related noun in -sa, the quality of being tematai. The scan gives the bare form without a Portuguese gloss; nothing is invented to fill the open space.
Tematoo is the accompanying adverbial form, with a clearly downward caron. It is printed alone beneath Temataſa, and both the indentation and absence of a gloss are preserved.
Temashi, temashina, and temasarina describe a person superior in manual work. The headword variants are linked by l, meaning or; Peßoa starts the Portuguese definition continued below.

runs.text: que excede a outro em obras de mãos.

lines.note: Completes the definition as someone surpassing another in manual work. Teuo- starts the contrasting Japanese term on the following row, with the printed division retained.
Completes Teuotori, the contrasted term for being inferior in manual skill. He o contrario explicitly marks it as the opposite, not another equivalent of Temaxi.

runs.text: Couſa que toca, ou pertence a alguẽ,

lines.note: Temae here denotes something concerning or belonging to a person. The range is broader than physical position in front of oneself, as the ensuing work and means examples show.
Adds the work a person does to the definition of temae. Sonata no temae begins the example identifying something as the other person's task or turn, divided after tema-.

runs.text: A vos pertence eſta obra, ou eſta he a

lines.note: Completes sonata no temae ja: this work belongs to you, or this is your turn. The Portuguese gives both interpretations, with the second continuing below.
Voſſa vez finishes the preceding example as your turn. Temae isogashii begins the next example, being busy with one's own work or affairs.

runs.text: ocupado com algũa couſa, ou obra propria.

lines.note: Completes the explanation of temae isogashii: occupied with some personal matter or work. The nasal abbreviation in algũa remains over u.
Temae ga naranu describes lacking the means for something. The Portuguese gloss starts not having the means, with pera divided after pe-.
Completes the lack-of-means definition. Temae doku then introduces work or a contract undertaken on one's own account; the phrase's detailed explanation follows.

runs.text: ou empreitada que hum toma à ſua conta a qual

lines.note: Describes a job or contract that a person takes on his own account. The final l of qual is present by the right rule and restores the relative pronoun truncated by the OCR.

runs.text: pode acabar quando quiſer ſem ter deuer mais

lines.note: The person can finish the undertaking when he wishes, with no further obligation or involvement. Mais is visible, correcting OCR mats; the closely set historical deuer is retained rather than silently respaced as modern de ver.
Completes the statement about having no further dealings with anything. Temae ni kane ga nai hodo ni begins the next example, explaining that the speaker currently has no money.

Completes hodo ni kashaserarei, a deferential request for a loan because the speaker has no money at hand. The abraded a in caſaxerarei is retained from the surviving form; the Portuguese explanation continues below.
Completes the example: since I currently have no silver or money, lend me some. Empreſtaime retains the printed joined pronoun construction.
Temaedoku refers back to the preceding Temaye entry and its contract-work sense. Vide is italic apparatus; the complete referenced Temaye is upright, correcting the OCR's style break inside the word.

runs.text: Modo, ou geito de ter, ou tomar

lines.note: Temochi here means the manner or ease of holding or taking something in the hand. The damaged initial is T, and geito, not OCR grito, is supported by the surviving vowel and the repeated wording below.

runs.text: algũa couſa nas mãos como pena, abano, &c.

lines.note: Gives a pen and a fan as examples of objects held in the hands. The fan is abano, with a visible b matching its earlier occurrence, rather than OCR ahano.
Temochi ga yoi or warui means that something handles well or badly. The alternative l is Latin or, and ru- begins Portuguese ruim on the next row.

runs.text: im geito de tomar: ou ter na mão algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes ruim and the explanation of a good or bad manner of grasping or holding an object. Geito corrects OCR gento, and the colon after tomar remains visible. The entry continues with a new figurative sense on f499; the separate ¶ Per. below anticipates that continuation.
